comparison: Perfect agreement on structure determination (C1, C35-C38). Both evaluations affirm the high-resolution cryo-EM structure at 2.30 Å with C1 symmetry revealing PSI monomer core and five FCPI subunits. Reviewers explicitly praise the exceptional resolution and structural quality.

Strong agreement on FCPI subunit identification (C2, C3, C39, C65). Both evaluations support the identification methodology based on characteristic amino acid residues and sequence analysis. Reviewers acknowledge these as novel subunits not previously seen in other diatoms.

Agreement on identification of novel subunits including Psa29 (C52-C58). Both evaluations support the structural characterization and phylogenetic analysis. Reviewers explicitly recognize subunits not previously identified in earlier reconstructions.

Agreement on cofactor composition identification (C41, C42, C69-C74, C76, C77). Both evaluations support the identification of chlorophylls and carotenoids including the novel β-carotene binding. Reviewers affirm pigments not previously seen were revealed by the high-resolution structure.

Agreement on protein-protein interactions between FCPI-1 and PSI subunits (C4, C5, C80-C85). Both evaluations support the detailed characterization of interactions at stromal and lumenal sides. Reviewers explicitly affirm the revelation of protein-protein interactions not previously seen, enabled by the high resolution.

Agreement on FCPI-2 interactions with PsaB and PsaM (C104-C107). OpenEval provides detailed residue-level analysis while peer reviewers affirm the broader identification of protein-protein interactions and molecular details of FCP arrangement.

Agreement on FCPI-3 interactions with PsaL (C108-C111). OpenEval details specific interactions while peer reviewers support the overall elucidation of molecular details and protein-protein interactions revealed by the structure.

Agreement on FCPI-4 and FCPI-5 interactions (C112-C117). OpenEval provides specific residue analysis while peer reviewers affirm the comprehensive identification of protein-protein interactions and FCP arrangement details.

Agreement on molecular assembly mechanism (C118-C122, C137-C140). Both evaluations support the lock-and-key binding mechanism based on specific amino acid residues. Peer reviewers describe this as 'convincing evidence' and 'interesting speculation' about assembly mechanisms.

Agreement on comparative phylogenetic analysis (C123-C129). Both evaluations support the structural comparison between T. pseudonana and C. gracilis showing conserved binding sites and orthology. Reviewers explicitly affirm the phylogenetic analyses provide convincing evidence of conserved motifs.

Agreement on non-homology at FCPI-4 site (C130, C131). Both evaluations support the finding that TpLhcf10 is not homologous to CgLhcf3, indicating different interaction mechanisms. This is part of the broader comparative analysis affirmed by reviewers.

Agreement on conserved loop structures and protein motifs in RedCAPs (C95-C103, C102, C103). Both evaluations support the identification of conserved amino acids and the inference about binding contribution. Reviewers affirm the phylogenetic evidence for conserved motifs crucial for FCPI binding.

Agreement on evolutionary conservation of protein motifs (C6, C102, C103, C126-C129). Both evaluations support the selective binding mechanism and its evolutionary implications. Reviewers provide 'convincing evidence' for conserved motifs through structural, sequence, and phylogenetic analyses.

Agreement on lock-and-key mechanism and assembly principles (C137-C140). Both evaluations support the mechanistic interpretation of selective FCPI binding. Reviewers affirm this as convincing evidence with interesting speculation about assembly mechanisms.

Agreement on broader implications for PSI-LHCI assembly (C141-C143). Both evaluations support the applicability to other organisms and evolutionary significance. Reviewers explicitly state the findings have implications for related PSI-LHCI supercomplexes in plants and advance multiple research fields.

Agreement on Psa29 functional uncertainty (C60-C63). Both evaluations support the structural identification while acknowledging unclear functional role. Reviewers implicitly support this by noting findings 'set the stage for functional experiments,' aligning with the call for mutagenesis studies.

Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN regarding CgRedCAP binding in C. gracilis (C86-C94). OpenEval notes the speculation based on sequence similarity but acknowledges it remains unclear. Peer reviewers do not specifically address this uncertainty but their 'interesting speculation' comment may encompass it.

Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN regarding the difference in FCPI subunit numbers between species (C132-C136). OpenEval notes unclear reasons with speculative explanations. Peer reviewers do not specifically comment on this question despite affirming overall structural findings.

OpenEval evaluates PSI core subunit identification and the unidentified 'Unknown' subunit (C43-C51). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this finding, though it is part of the overall structural characterization that reviewers affirm.

Partial overlap on β-carotene identification (C75-C79). OpenEval discusses excitation-energy-transfer pathways and β-carotene binding to FCPI-1/RedCAP. Peer reviewers affirm pigment identification generally but do not specifically evaluate the energy transfer pathway proposals or functional uncertainty.

OpenEval evaluates cofactor differences in PSI core between T. pseudonana and C. gracilis (C145-C148). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these comparative cofactor findings.

OpenEval evaluates background/contextual claims about photosynthesis and diatoms (C7-C34). These are established literature citations providing context. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these are not novel findings requiring assessment.

OpenEval evaluates methodological details about T. pseudonana growth conditions (C144). This is standard methodology for reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation as reviewers do not typically assess routine methodological details.
